title: DAO Recordset.RecordCount returns only the number of rows visited until a MoveLast forces a full table walk. Legacy code uses MoveLast / MoveFirst as a sentinel; modern providers don't need it
sourceContent:
Attribute VB_Name = "modOrderStats"
Option Explicit

' DAO Recordset.RecordCount returns only the number of rows the cursor
' has actually touched. To get the true count, code from the 1990s
' issues MoveLast (to force a full walk) THEN MoveFirst (to reset).
' On Jet / MDB this works; on ADO and EF Core this idiom is a no-op
' AND a performance trap on large tables.

Public Function CountOrders(db As DAO.Database, customerId As Long) As Long
    Dim rs As DAO.Recordset
    Set rs = db.OpenRecordset("SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE CustomerId = " & customerId)
    If rs.EOF Then
        CountOrders = 0
    Else
        rs.MoveLast      ' Force the cursor through every row
        rs.MoveFirst     ' Reset for any downstream walk
        CountOrders = rs.RecordCount
    End If
    rs.Close
End Function

canonicalInputs.rationale: EOF on open; MoveLast/MoveFirst NOT executed; returns 0 directly.
MoveLast forces a 5-row walk; RecordCount returns 5; MoveFirst resets the cursor for any caller.
Same logic; on a 200k-row table MoveLast walks all of them — measurable latency the modern port should NOT inherit.

notes: Idiom-driven trap. EF Core's CountAsync() or a SELECT COUNT(*) query is the correct .NET 10 equivalent — there's no cursor to walk and no MoveLast/MoveFirst dance to preserve. The extraction MUST emit (a) the com_interop_contract identifying DAO, (b) at least one late_binding_call covering rs.MoveLast / rs.MoveFirst, (c) a default_property_usage for RecordCount (it's a default property on the recordset surface), (d) two edge_cases (empty set + large-table perf), and (e) an open_question naming SELECT COUNT / EF Core CountAsync as the modern replacement. A spec that translates MoveLast / MoveFirst literally to EF Core is the worst calibration miss for this trap.
